newsitem.title: PERU: Peru government and rebels relaunch hostage talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru government and rebels relaunch hostage talks.

text.p: Peru's government and Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home on Tuesday began face-to-face talks at a nearby safe house in hopes of finding a peaceful end to the standoff.

A rebel believed to be the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's (MRTA) second-in-command, Rolly Rojas, laid down his weapons and left the building for the first time since the siege began Dec. 17, 1996, to meet Peru's negotiator Domingo Palermo.
A white Red Cross car ferried the rebel the 150 feet (50 metres) out of the the fortified diplomatic compound and across the street to the specially rented two-story home.
"We assume Rojas has gone in and the talks have started. That was the plan, and from what I saw, everything went according to that plan," Red Cross official Cecile Baux told Reuters.

President Alberto Fujimori said he hoped the meeting -- the first direct talks between the apparently intransigent sides since Dec. 28, 1996, -- would pave the way for an end to the eight-week crisis.

"Now these conversations are beginning, I would say that there are elements that give us a certain optimism," Fujimori told Peruvian reporters in London. "(Rojas) is a sociologist familiar with the theme and he could help us find a solution."

Fujimori said the talks with Rojas, a 34-year-old former busfare collector who goes by the nom de guerre "El Arabe" -- The Arab -- should lead to formal negotiations in the next few weeks with rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini.

Special police force officers in neighbouring homes surveyed the talks' safe house while sharpshooters on nearby roofs trained their rifles on the building. The Red Cross erected a huge flag emblazoned with their logo on the roof of the house to show they guaranteed the safety of negotiators.

Police also tightened security in the area. They pushed hordes of journalists behind security lines to a distance of three blocks from the talks and restricted access to the zone with vehicle and dog patrols. Plainclothes police mingled among the journalists.

Talks had been on hold since Palermo entered the besieged ambassador's home Dec. 28 because of the government's refusal to consider the rebels' main demand for the release of hundreds of jailed comrades.

A commission overseeing the talks -- including representatives from the Red Cross, the Vatican and Canada as well as a Japanese government observer -- said in a statement it hoped the meeting would bring "a prompt and peaceful solution to the current problem with absolute respect for lives and human dignity."
The commission members, who were present at the talks, said the two sides agreed to a pact of silence over the content of the discussions.
The resumption of talks raised hopes for an early end to the siege. "I do believe we are entering the home stretch," Peru's ombudsman, Jorge Santistevan de Noriega, told local television.

Outside the residence in the middle-class leafy district of San Isidro, members of a Peruvian workers' union laid on the floor a large, blue banner with messages in English, French and Spanish saying: "Dialogue to save human lives."

But Tuesday's talks promised to be tough. The MRTA said it would not drop its demand for the release of its jailed comrades. And despite his optimism, Fujimori again flatly rejected that demand and ruled out any ransom payments.

"The beginning of talks does not necessarily mean the start of a solution to the conflict," rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini said on Monday via walkie-talkie. He accused Fujimori of seeking to use the talks as a "psychological weapon," charging that he had issued a "veiled threat" to use force against the rebels if negotiations fail.

The rebels originally took more than 500 hostages during a lavish cocktail party at the diplomatic mansion but have freed most of them. The remaining 72 captives in the mined and booby- trapped residence include two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and Fujimori's brother.
